paragraphs.heading: A cloud where molecules form
paragraphs.text: A molecular cloud is a kind of interstellar cloud dense and large enough for molecules to form inside it, most often molecular hydrogen, H₂. When stars are forming in it, it is sometimes called a stellar nursery. That sets it apart from other parts of the interstellar medium, where the gas is mostly ionized. Hydrogen is the most abundant kind of atom in these clouds, and under the right conditions it forms the H₂ molecule.

paragraphs.heading: The invisible ingredient
paragraphs.text: Even though there is so much of it, H₂ is hard to detect. Its molecule is symmetrical, so its rotation and vibration modes are weak, which makes it almost invisible to direct observation. Astronomers instead track carbon monoxide (CO), which is much easier to detect thanks to its rotational energy and lopsided structure. They treat the ratio between CO brightness and H₂ mass as constant, though there are reasons to doubt this for some other galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Where they sit in our galaxy
paragraphs.text: In the Milky Way, molecular clouds fill under one percent of the interstellar medium's volume, yet they are its densest part. Most of the molecular gas lies in a ring 3.5 to 7.5 kiloparsecs (11,000 to 24,000 light-years) from the galactic centre; the Sun is about 8.5 kiloparsecs out. Large CO maps show this gas lines up with the spiral arms. That suggests the clouds form and break apart in under 10 million years, the time material takes to pass through an arm.

paragraphs.heading: Listening for hydrogen
paragraphs.text: The search for these clouds grew out of radio astronomy. During World War II, Henk van de Hulst worked out that neutral hydrogen atoms should send out a radio signal strong enough to detect. When the spins of the atom's proton and electron flip from parallel to antiparallel, a lower-energy state, the atom releases a spectral line at 1420.405 MHz, known as the 21 cm line. In 1951 two groups found it within months: Ewen and Purcell in March, and Muller and Oort in May.

paragraphs.heading: From molecules to clouds
paragraphs.text: Radio astronomers then began hunting for molecules between the stars. Alan Barrett and Sander Weinreb of MIT found OH in 1963 in the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, the first interstellar molecule detected at radio wavelengths. NH₃ followed in 1968, then formaldehyde and molecular hydrogen in 1969. In 1970 Arno Penzias and his team detected CO near the galactic centre, including in the giant molecular cloud Sagittarius B2, the first molecular cloud ever detected.

paragraphs.heading: Where stars start
paragraphs.text: Inside a molecular cloud are denser regions called clumps, holding much dust and many gas cores. If gravity is strong enough to make a clump's dust and gas collapse, star formation begins there. Interest in these clouds has kept growing: a paper published in 2022 counts over 10,000 molecular clouds found since Sagittarius B2.
